text: The New York Times names five hard rules for crossword construction: black square symmetry, all-over interlock, no unchecked squares, a minimum answer length of three letters, and black squares used in moderation.

The NYT symmetry rule is stated as black square symmetry which typically comes in the form of 180-degree rotational symmetry, naming 180-degree rotation as the usual instance of a broader requirement rather than as the only permitted symmetry.
The NYT word-count ceilings are 78 words for a 15x15, 72 for a themeless 15x15, and 140 for a 21x21, exceedable slightly at the editor's discretion.
The NYT submission specification names only 15x15 and 21x21 as its grid sizes, in both its word-count and payment tables.
Theme entries must be paired at equal length at 180-degree rotated positions, so committing to a ten-letter theme entry obligates a second ten-letter theme entry in the mirrored slot.
support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; entity mismatch

text: An unpairable theme entry is relocated to the grid's line of self-symmetry rather than dropped: a 13-letter entry centred in a 15-column grid forces one black square at each end of its row.
support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; entity mismatch

text: Asymmetrical theme-related short entries are conventionally rejected rather than tolerated.
Placing the first theme entry in the third row is a convention rather than a codified rule, and sources state it with hedging language such as 'usually'.
The stated reason for the row-3 convention is maximum separation between theme answers, which constructors adopt to increase the likelihood that the grid fills well.
The row-3 convention is overridden when it would create a band of three-letter words, because the word list offers far fewer three-letter than four-letter options.
No source retrieved gave a fixed numeric row-gap rule between theme rows; spacing is governed indirectly through the theme-square budget and the word-count ceiling.
Theme entries may cross one another, but crossing them makes the surrounding fill harder and is conventionally avoided.
The published black-square method is forced-then-aesthetic: place the blocks that the theme entries' endpoints force, plus any blocks those force in turn, and only then shape the interior.

Most 15x15 grids resolve into roughly nine sections joined by two or three longer connector words, and diagonal block runs are preferred to straight horizontal or vertical runs because they fill more easily.
High-Scrabble-value letters in a theme entry are placed toward the edges rather than the centre, because a central hard letter interacts with more other theme material.
Given a hard consonant, the black square is positioned so that the crossing word begins with that letter rather than ending with it.
The choice of which letter of a placed entry to block after is made on letter-position frequency in the word list, preferring the letter that more words end in.
Long non-theme bonus entries are conventionally placed in the Down direction so solvers do not mistake them for theme material.
Word-count ceilings differ by publication and by editor; 21x21 maxima reported for individual editors range from 140 to 146.
The LAT, WSJ and Universal word-count figures reported here are a secondhand transcription of those publishers' specifications, not a first-hand retrieval of them.

XWord Info hosts no theme-placement or grid-design tutorial; its constructor-facing pages document the site's own tools and define puzzle statistics such as word count, cheater squares and open squares.
Crossword Fiend carries no construction-placement guidance; its only construction-tagged post is a mentoring-directory announcement and its substance is puzzle review and solver ratings.
Anbulagan and Botea 2008 is 'Crossword Puzzles as a Constraint Problem', CP 2008, LNCS 5202, pages 550-554, DOI 10.1007/978-3-540-85958-1_40.

On 9x9 grids, with the word list grown 1 percent (2,200 words) at a time, hard crossword instances occur in a phase-transition band running from roughly 10,000 to 35,000 words; the paper names the benchmark dictionary as 220,000 words in its separate blocked-cell experiment.
support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; entity mismatch

text: The hard dictionary-size band widens with grid size, reaching roughly 22,000 to 110,000 words on 23x23 grids.
Varying the number of blocked cells at a fixed grid size produces the same three-region structure of unsatisfiable, hard, and satisfiable instances.

Botea and Anbulagan 2009 introduce a model-counting formula for the expected number of solutions of a crossword instance, computable from the grid's slot-length counts and the dictionary's word-length histogram together with two probability factors.
support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; year mismatch; entity mismatch

text: The expected-solution-count estimate converts to a hardness prediction through the identity that search effort to a first solution is approximately the effort to exhaust the search space divided by the number of solutions.

The intersection-constraint probability factor in the crossword model-counting formula has no principled estimator: the uniform-letter independence estimate proved inaccurate, the authors calibrate it empirically against exactly-counted small instances, and they state that finding a better formula remains open.

Constrainedness kappa is defined as one minus the base-two logarithm of the expected number of solutions divided by the number of binary state variables, and the soluble/insoluble transition sits near kappa of one.
Constrainedness is a property of an ensemble defined by a generation method, not of a single problem instance.

NP-complete problem classes admit at least one order parameter whose critical value separates an over-constrained mostly-insoluble region from an under-constrained mostly-soluble region, with search cost peaking at the critical value.
Ginsberg, Frank, Halpin and Torrance 1990 is a construction paper: it reports a program that generates crossword puzzles.
support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; year mismatch; entity mismatch

text: The cheapest-first heuristic orders slots by a compile-time statistical estimate of the number of choices remaining, while dynamic search rearrangement counts the remaining possibilities at run time.
Ordering slots by exact run-time counts was found to be far more efficient than ordering them by the compile-time statistical estimate.
The least-constraining-value rule for crosswords scores each candidate word by the product, over the unfilled crossing slots, of their remaining-candidate counts, and selects the maximiser.
Only the first ten candidate words for a slot need be scored under the least-constraining-value rule, and the overhead of that scoring is repaid only on grids of 9x9 and larger.
The most-constrained-slot heuristic rests on a fail-first argument that assumes slot independence, an assumption crosswords violate by construction.
Singleton arc consistency is a complete decision procedure for solvability only on constraint languages of bounded width, characterised by five forbidden binary micro-structure patterns.

Because crossword word-compatibility relations are arbitrary same-length dictionary subsets, propagation on a crossword region proves unsatisfiability by domain wipeout but certifies nothing when domains survive.

Filling crosswords remains NP-hard under extremely severe structural restrictions on the intersection graph, and the treewidth-parameterised algorithm cannot be improved to fixed-parameter tractability under the Exponential Time Hypothesis.

Empirical hardness models fit a supervised model from cheaply computable instance features to predicted solver runtime, and are defined over such features rather than over any particular problem domain.

A convolutional network taking only the black-cell pattern as input, encoded as a matrix with black cells at plus 0.5 and empty cells at minus 0.5, was trained to predict the score a crossword filler would achieve.
On 100 held-out grids the learned predictor reached a Spearman rank correlation of minus 0.64 against the filler's actual score, compared with minus 0.24 for the maximum-word-slot-length baseline.
The learned-proxy result was obtained under Romanian competition rules, which impose no rotational symmetry, cap black cells at 26 on a 13x13 grid, and permit slots of length one and two.
support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; entity mismatch

text: In the standard construction model a variable is a slot, its domain is the set of words that fit it, and constraint propagation shrinks the domains of uninstantiated slots as words are placed.
A search deliberately run with an unreachably high target score, and therefore expected to fail, still yields a best partial grid usable as the seed for a second search at an achievable target.

The only explicit numeric density objective published for crossword grids is the count of intersections multiplied by the letter density of the bounding box, with a reported mean intersections-to-letters ratio of 13.95 percent.
Maximising a crossing-count-times-density objective produced puzzles the authors describe as unsolvable by humans in reasonable time.
Mazlack 1976 is 'Computer construction of crossword puzzles using precedence relationships', Artificial Intelligence volume 7 issue 1, pages 1 to 19, DOI 10.1016/0004-3702(76)90019-9.
support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; year mismatch; entity mismatch

text: The full text of Mazlack 1976 is available only through purchase or institutional sign-in at the publisher; the abstract is free.
support_notes: number mismatch; year mismatch; entity mismatch

text: Mazlack 1976 concerns letter-by-letter construction, dictionary structure and access, and dynamic ordering and reordering of the solution sequence; its abstract does not mention black squares, symmetry, or pre-placed entries.
support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; year mismatch; entity mismatch

text: Across the academic construction line the blocked-cell pattern is an input to the algorithm rather than something the algorithm chooses, stated explicitly as a constraint that no blocked cells may be added or removed during the process.
Botea and Bulitko's 2021 SoCS paper restricts itself to the word-adding half of its task and lists generating good configurations of black cells as future work.
support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; year mismatch; entity mismatch

text: The same authors' 2021 CoG paper does generate black-cell configurations, using a genetic algorithm that shifts black cells to neighbouring empty squares under adjacency and connectivity constraints, with a learned proxy as the fitness function.
support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; year mismatch

text: The constraints enforced in that black-cell evolution are that no two black cells are cardinally adjacent and that the empty region stays fully connected; rotational symmetry is not among them.
Black-square mask generation under connectivity constraints has been shown NP-complete, in a Swedish-style setting that carries no rotational-symmetry requirement.

XWordGiver places a required word and then writes black squares at both ends along its axis, tracked against a selectable 180-degree point-symmetry rule flag, but its own documentation states it is optimised for Japanese crossword generation.
support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; entity mismatch

text: PuzzlePlot generates a crossword from supplied words with a stated guarantee of symmetrical layout, a single connected region, minimum entry length three and zero unchecked cells, but is unpublished hobby code with no algorithmic analysis.
Agarwal and Joshi's unconstrained generation work determines both word locations and grid geometry from a fixed vocabulary, but contains no mention of symmetry.
There are 404,139,015,237,875 connected, 180-degree-symmetric, minimum-length-three 15x15 grids whose white region touches every edge, and 409,764,131,469,788 without that last requirement.
support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; entity mismatch

text: Brute-force enumeration of valid 5x5 grids gives 12 under 180-degree rotational symmetry, 2 under 90-degree rotation, 6 horizontal, 6 vertical and 26 diagonal.
support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; entity mismatch

text: A multigraph formalisation exists whose necessary conditions correspond to the five American structure rules, but its authors leave the counting step itself as future work.

Perfect crossword grids, meaning grids with no black cells at all, are generated using one trie per word length with each node carrying a 26-bit code so an intersection can be tested by a bitwise AND.
support_notes: low lexical overlap; number mismatch; entity mismatch

text: Construction tools rank which slot to fill next and which word to place in a given slot, but almost none rank where in the grid a given entry should go.
The author of Ingrid states in his own documentation that placing black squares and theme entries remains a manual process and that he is aware of no construction tool that automates it.

Crossword Compiler's 'Fit theme words' feature scans grid patterns for places a list of theme words will fit and lets the constructor choose among the arrangements, which is an enumeration rather than a scored ranking.
CrossFire's 'Best Location' is a slot-ordering feature that selects a constrained word giving the most value in the filling process, not a ranking of positions for a supplied entry.

CrossFire's visible scoring inputs are a dictionary Word Score, a per-word Grid Score measuring the quality of the immediate neighbourhood with values above 0.9 considered good, a Final Score for a completed fill, and an XScore ranking placed words by crossing quality.
Ingrid's open-source core maintains arc consistency with AC-3 and orders slots with a dom/wdeg variant, computing slot priority as the remaining option count divided by an accrued slot weight.
CrossHatch scores a fill candidate as the sum of its cross score and minimum cross score, multiplied by its word score, multiplied by a factor of 100 unless the word is outside the word list.
Ingrid's 'Recommended' sort balances word score, letter score and a factor based on how many options remain in the crossing slots, and is documented as not being based on full-grid fill quality.
Exet ranks unfilled slots by how few viable fill suggestions remain and provides a keyboard jump to the most constrained slot.
Exet supports a US-style doubly checked grid mode and branches its grid-completion logic on the American all-cells-checked format, so its fill and ranking mechanics apply to American construction.

Phil has no candidate-ranking or position-scoring feature: its fill engine is a SAT solver that returns one satisfying assignment, and a search of its fill-logic source for score, rank, candidate, heatmap and best returned no matches.
Qxw presents a feasible-character list at the cursor ordered from most to least promising.
Crosserville highlights a slot yellow at ten or fewer candidates, yellow with the sole candidate shown when exactly one remains, and red at zero, leaving slots with more than ten candidates unmarked.
Crosserville's candidate counts are computed from raw pattern matching rather than confirmed-valid options, so a counted candidate can still be a dead end.

Exet's viability indicator is log-scaled rather than tiered: zero candidates renders purple at the largest radius, one to fifteen render red with radius shrinking as the base-two logarithm of the count rises, and sixteen or more renders fully transparent.

Qxw draws hotspot dots sized so that a bigger dot means fewer possibilities, with a distinct marker at exactly one remaining possibility and a question mark at zero, and gives no numeric thresholds for the size scaling in its manual.
CrossFire's per-cell overlay shows a forced letter in dark grey at one possibility, shows the letters in miniature between two and nine possibilities, and shows nothing at ten or more.
Crossword Compiler's Grid Insight surfaces a single binary green or red fillability indicator for a grid section rather than a graduated per-cell or per-slot candidate-count overlay.

CrossHatch's cell colouring encodes the quality tier of the word already placed rather than the candidate count of an unfilled slot, and its README describes three tiers while its source implements a five-value enumeration.

Every nytimes.com crossword-construction URL tried returned a 771-byte DataDome bot-challenge body to HTTP clients including curl with a browser User-Agent, WebFetch, a text-extraction proxy and the Wayback Machine, while a real Chrome session rendered the pages in full.

The MDPI article and PDF URLs, and the DOI redirect to them, returned HTTP 403 with a roughly 400-byte edge-CDN denial body to HTTP clients, while a real Chrome session rendered the full open-access article.
ResearchGate returned HTTP 403 to an HTTP client with a browser User-Agent and was not tested in a browser, so nothing here establishes what it holds.

text: Two independent sources agree that when a theme entry contains a hard consonant, the black square should be positioned so that the crossing word begins with that letter rather than ending with it.
Roughly half of all words containing a J begin with it, and more than a hundred times as many words start with J as end with one.
An X is better placed in the middle of an entry than at either end, a letter-specific exception to the begins-rather-than-ends rule.
Constructors are advised to avoid small isolated sections of words reachable by only one entry.
Every construction rule including symmetry can be violated, but the more significant the rule the better the justification required.
Salomon gives a 15x15 norm of three or four theme entries totalling between 40 and 45 theme squares, and calls 80 theme squares the bare minimum for a 21x21.
